steps.body:
The sine wave's slope is the cosine wave. Not approximately — exactly.

**(sin x)′ = cos x** · **(cos x)′ = −sin x**

Differentiate four times and you are back where you started. The derivatives go round in a circle, which is precisely what you would expect of a function born on one.
Read the slope off the wave.
explanationVariants: (sin x)′ = cos x, and cos 0 = 1. At the origin the sine wave is climbing at exactly 45°.
That slope of exactly 1 at the origin is why radians are the only sane unit for calculus — in degrees the answer would carry an ugly π/180.

commonErrors.feedback: That is sin 0, the HEIGHT of the wave at the origin. Its SLOPE there is cos 0 = 1 — the wave is climbing steeply.
That would be the slope where the wave is falling fastest, at x = π. At 0 it is rising: cos 0 = +1.
That is the answer in DEGREES, and it is why calculus insists on radians: only in radians does (sin x)′ come out as a clean cos x.

steps.body: The wave and the circle, one more time.

widget.prompt: Rotate to 90°. Watch the HEIGHT (the sine) and think about how fast it is changing.
widget.successFeedback: At 90° the height is at its maximum of 1 — and precisely there, it has momentarily stopped changing: the sine wave is flat at its crest. And indeed cos 90° = 0. The derivative of the height is the horizontal coordinate, which is the cosine. The two functions were never separate.
widget.lowFeedback: Not far enough — the height is still climbing, so its derivative is still positive.
widget.highFeedback: Past 90°, and the height has started to fall — its derivative has gone negative.

predict.prompt: You'll rotate from 0° to 90°. What does the point's HEIGHT do along the way?
predict.reveal: From 0° to 90° the height — the sine — only rises; the fall doesn't begin until past 90° (or past 270° coming out of the trough).

cml.actionGoal: Move the angle and coordinate the circle point, triangle ratios, and trigonometric values.

explanationVariants: (cos x)′ = −sin x. At x = 0, sin 0 = 0, so the slope is 0 — the cosine wave is flat at its crest.
The minus sign is not decoration: just past 0 the cosine is falling, so its derivative must be negative there.

widget.prompt: Why does (cos x)′ = −sin x carry a minus sign?

options.label: Cosine falls just right of zero while sine is positive.
options.feedback: Right. The minus is forced by the geometry: cosine starts at its peak and goes DOWN, while sine is climbing.

options.label: Cosine rises just right of zero while sine is positive.
options.feedback: cos x is positive for x near 0. The sign in the derivative is about the DIRECTION the curve is heading, not the sign of its height.

options.label: Cosine is negative just right of zero, so its slope is negative.
options.feedback: It is forced. Drop the minus and the formula would claim the cosine is RISING just after its peak, which the graph plainly refutes.

options.label: Sine is zero just right of zero, so cosine cannot fall.
options.feedback: They are — and that shift explains why the derivative is the OTHER function, but not why the sign flips. The flip comes from the direction of travel.

steps.body:
The rest of the library follows from the quotient and chain rules:

**(tan x)′ = sec² x** — always positive, which is why the tangent graph only ever climbs.

And with an inside: **(sin u)′ = cos u · u′**. The inner derivative is owed here exactly as everywhere else.

explanationVariants: The wave is squashed to half its width, so it climbs twice as fast — and the derivative reports exactly that.

commonErrors.feedback: That is cos(2x) at x = 0 — the outside only. The chain rule owes you the inner derivative, 2.
sin 2x is steeply RISING at the origin, not flat. Its derivative there is 2cos 0 = 2.
You may have divided by the inner derivative rather than multiplying. The chain rule multiplies: cos(2x) × 2.

hints: This is a PRODUCT: u = x, v = sin x. So the product rule comes first.
f′ = 1·sin x + x·cos x = sin x + x cos x.
At x = 0: sin 0 = 0 and cos 0 = 1, so the answer is 0 + 0 × 1.
explanationVariants: f′ = sin x + x cos x. At x = 0 that is 0 + 0(1) = 0.
Both terms vanish at the origin — the first because sin 0 = 0, the second because of the factor x. The curve is momentarily flat there.

commonErrors.feedback: That is cos 0 — but the x·cos x term carries a factor of x, which is 0 here. And sin 0 = 0 too, so the whole derivative vanishes.
That would need both terms to contribute 1. In fact both contribute 0 at the origin.
Check the product rule: 1·sin x + x·cos x. No minus sign appears anywhere.

widget.fallbackFeedback: f′ = sin x + x cos x → at 0: 0 + 0 = 0.

steps.body: The derivatives go round in a circle.
takeaways: (sin x)′ = cos x and (cos x)′ = −sin x. Four differentiations return you to the start.
The minus sign is forced: cosine starts at a peak and falls.
Radians are not a preference. In degrees, (sin x)′ picks up a factor of π/180 and every formula turns ugly.
steps.teaser: Last lesson: the derivative of an inverse, for free.

concept.body: Learn the pair, and the sign. **sin → cos** (no minus). **cos → −sin** (minus). Then differentiate four times and check that you return to where you began — if you do not, a sign has gone astray.

explanationVariants: (sin x)′ = cos x, and at x = π/3 (60°) that is cos 60° = 0.5.
No minus sign on this one — sine differentiates cleanly to cosine.

widget.prompt: f(x) = sin x. Find f′(π/3), as a decimal.

commonErrors.feedback: That is sin(π/3), the height. The slope is cos(π/3) = 0.5.
There is no minus sign when differentiating SINE. The minus belongs to cosine.
